cues.text: Let's work through the archived pre-test revision, starting with a question on version control and then moving to one on distributed teams.
First, Pre-test Question 7.
The question reads: An effective version control strategy allows teams to, blank.
There are four options.
Option one: deliver tasks via printed reports for traceability.
Option two: track changes, collaborate on files, and manage parallel development streams.
Option three: edit shared folders without tracking history.
Option four: avoid peer reviews and accelerate deployment.
The LMS-reviewed answer is option two: track changes, collaborate on files, and manage parallel development streams.
Here is the supplied explanation.
Version control preserves history and coordinates parallel changes; peer review remains valuable.
Let's see why that fits.
Version control is about keeping a record of how files change over time, and about letting several people work on those files together.
That is why the correct option has three parts: tracking changes, collaborating on files, and managing parallel development streams.
Option one, printed reports, has nothing to do with version control; traceability here comes from the preserved history.
Option three describes the opposite of version control, because editing shared folders without tracking history throws away exactly what version control provides.
And option four fails because, as the explanation says, peer review remains valuable.
Version control does not replace it or remove the need for it.
Now Pre-test Question 8.
The question reads: Distributed development teams benefit from asynchronous tools primarily because they, blank.
Again there are four options.
Option one: eliminate the need for formal task descriptions.
Option two: speed up urgent bug fixes in real-time.
Option three: allow individuals to work across time zones without communication breakdown.
Option four: prevent the need for any team meetings.
The LMS-reviewed answer is option three: allow individuals to work across time zones without communication breakdown.
The supplied explanation says: Asynchronous communication avoids requiring simultaneous presence across time zones; urgent coordination may still be synchronous.
Let's unpack that.
In a distributed team, members may be in different time zones, so they are not all online at the same moment.
Asynchronous tools let one person leave a message, a task update, or a comment, and a colleague respond later, when their working day begins.
Nobody has to be present at the same time, and that is how communication keeps flowing without breaking down.
Now look at why the other options fall short.
Option one claims asynchronous tools eliminate formal task descriptions.
Nothing in the source supports that.
Option two says they speed up urgent bug fixes in real time, but real-time work is synchronous by nature, and the explanation specifically notes that urgent coordination may still be synchronous.
Option four says they prevent the need for any team meetings.
That goes too far; the source makes no such claim, and the word "any" is an absolute that the source does not support.
So the contrast to remember is this.
Version control preserves history and coordinates parallel work, while peer review stays valuable.
Asynchronous tools remove the need for simultaneous presence across time zones, while urgent matters may still need synchronous coordination.
